subtitle: "Root eighths, down-up strumming and a backbeat"

[Open the Straight-eighth rock style in the Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.html?style=rock){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

## What it is

The basic rock band: drums with a snare **backbeat** on 2 and 4 and even eighth notes on the hi-hat, an
electric bass on the root in eighths, and guitar strumming every eighth note.

## A little history

Rhythm and blues of the late 1940s and early '50s was mostly shuffled (swung) eighths. Through the 1950s,
records by Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Ray Charles mixed straight eighths in, and by the early 1960s
even eighths were the norm in rock and soul; Alexander Stewart traces the shift through New Orleans
drummers such as Earl Palmer. The backbeat came from gospel handclaps and R&B. The British Invasion, then
punk's down-stroke eighths (the Ramones, 1976) and new wave, kept the plain driving eighths at the centre
of the style.

## The band's version

- **Bass:** *Root eighths*. **Comping:** down-up eighths on the guitar. **Drums:** a backbeat whose kick
  varies from bar to bar. Chords are **pushed** (they arrive an eighth early) the way rock bands do.

## Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Little Richard, *Lucille* | 1957 | Often cited as an early straight-eighth rock and roll record. |
| Chuck Berry, *Johnny B. Goode* | 1958 | The guitar boogie that became rock rhythm guitar. |
| The Kinks, *You Really Got Me* | 1964 | Power chords and driving eighths. |
| Ramones, *Blitzkrieg Bop* | 1976 | Eighths on everything. |
| U2, *With or Without You* | 1987 | Adam Clayton's root eighths, the whole song. |

### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| The Strokes, *Last Nite* | 2001 | Garage-rock eighths on guitar and bass. |
| The Killers, *Mr. Brightside* | 2003 | Driving eighths the whole song. |
| Arctic Monkeys, *I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor* | 2005 | Fast straight eighths and a backbeat. |

## Sources

- Alexander Stewart, "'Funky Drummer': New Orleans, James Brown and the rhythmic transformation of American
  popular music", *Popular Music* 19/3 (2000).
- Robert Palmer, *Rock & Roll: An Unruly History* (Harmony, 1995).
